# Preface {.unnumbered}

Most research code outlives a semester: new dependencies, shared repos, experiments
to reproduce, and collaborators who were not there for the first script. Many students
still arrive with homework habits — a few files, no version control, no package layout,
and no plan after the deadline.

Robotics widens the gap. The **ecosystem is fragmented**: MuJoCo next to Isaac,
URDF/MJCF next to USD, ROS-adjacent tooling next to bare Python repos, `conda` next
to `uv`, sim next to hardware — every lab picks a different slice. People arrive from
mechanical engineering, EE, CS, or ML with uneven baselines; some have never left a
notebook terminal. Excellent **courses** teach models and control; open RL classes such as
[Berkeley CS285](http://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/) go deep on policies and
sample complexity — not on editable installs, git hygiene, quaternion conventions, or
getting `step()` to run headless on a cluster. The gap shows up fast: clone a repo,
sync the env, make `step()` run — before the interesting science starts.

This tutorial fills that workshop gap. It is onboarding for the `robotics` example
package and for **how to start, develop, organize, and maintain a research project**:
Python environments and imports, project structure, debugging, version control,
NumPy/PyTorch tensor work, and the robotics concepts in `src/robotics/` (kinematics,
rotations, simulators, IK, contact). It does **not** replace controls or RL coursework
— it is a **single coherent path** through the engineering layer those courses usually
skip, closer to [MIT's *The Missing Semester*](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/) than a
syntax cheat sheet, so you can run experiments, compare simulators sensibly, and
collaborate without re-learning the stack every rotation.

We stay **narrow and runnable** rather than cataloguing every framework: one small repo,
two simulators on the same MJCF, one IK registry — enough structure to transfer when
your lab moves on. Official install guides and APIs:
[References and external docs](references.qmd#references). Math: your coursework.

Chapters are short and self-contained; use the sidebar to navigate.

## How to use it

- Runnable examples: `scripts/`; library: `src/robotics/`. Setup once with `uv sync`,
  then `uv run python scripts/<name>.py`.
- Code blocks here are snippets; authoritative versions are under `scripts/` and `src/`.
- Tool and simulator links: [References](references.qmd#references).
- **Progress:** each `##` section has a **Done** checkbox (saved in this browser).
  Unread sections are highlighted in the page TOC; **red `!`** marks warning sections
  not yet done; the sidebar shows chapter status (blue / orange / ✓).

## Building these docs

```bash
uv sync                 # project env (numpy, einops)
quarto preview docs     # live-reloading local preview
quarto render docs      # build static HTML into docs/_site
```

Install the [Quarto CLI](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/) separately (not a Python package). See [References](references.qmd#version-control-and-publishing) for other tool install links.
